quote: Ist $x^{p^2}-px-p$ irreducibel nach dem Modul $(p^2, p$ [?]
english: Is $x^{p^2}-px-p$ irreducible with respect to the modulus $(p^2, p$?
topic: The page ends a remark about Poincaré polygons whose opposite circular arcs are carried into each other, then poses questions on the irreducibility of x^{p^2}-px-p modulo (p^2, p) and on decomposing functions of degree p into linear factors modulo powers of p.

triage.modern_statement: Take f(x) = x^{p^2} − p x − p in Z[x]. Is f irreducible modulo p^2? That is, can f be written in (Z/p^2Z)[x] as a product of two monic polynomials of positive degree? Hilbert wrote the modulus as the Kronecker-style module system '(p^2, p' and never closed the bracket. The second entry is unclear, so I read it as 'mod p^2', which is the only way it makes sense. Under that reading the question is about irreducibility over Z/p^2 of a polynomial that is ≡ x^n mod p and whose constant term is divisible by p but not by p^2. Such a polynomial is irreducible over Q and over Q_p as well.
triage.answered_by: This was already settled before Hilbert asked it, by the Schönemann–Eisenstein criterion (Schönemann 1846, Eisenstein 1850). Schönemann's version is a statement about congruences modulo p^2. f is ≡ x^{p^2} mod p, and its constant term −p is divisible by p but not by p^2. Suppose f ≡ g·h mod p^2 with g and h monic. Reducing mod p gives g ≡ x^a and h ≡ x^b, so both constant terms are divisible by p. Their product is then divisible by p^2, which contradicts the constant term −p. So f is irreducible mod p^2, and also over Q and Q_p. Hensel-type lifting (also anticipated by Schönemann) covers the related question on the page about factoring into linear factors modulo higher powers of p.

evidence.claim: Schönemann gave the criterion, including proofs, in an 1846 article, before Eisenstein's 1850 publication; the criterion is also called the Schönemann–Eisenstein criterion.

Schönemann's original formulation works with congruences modulo powers of p: a polynomial ≡ x^n mod p whose constant term is not divisible by p^2 is irreducible. He also showed that factorizations mod p lift uniquely modulo p^m, which is Hensel's lemma.
David Cox wrote a historical account of why Schönemann found the criterion first and why Eisenstein proved it.
Schönemann obtained Hensel's Lemma before Hensel, and stated Eisenstein's Criterion before Eisenstein.

triage.why: If the modulus means p^2, the answer is yes, and it follows directly from the classical Schönemann–Eisenstein argument, which was known before Hilbert wrote the note. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The answer is classical and the polynomial question is no longer researched, but confidence is only medium because Hilbert's modulus '(p^2, p' is cut off. If he meant some other module system, for example with a polynomial or a prime ideal as the second entry, the question could be different, and no source I found discusses this specific note.
